ref: Manuscript evidence: Otto, Prolegomena §II (Codex Parisinus 451) p. xiii; the Athenagoras and Arethas link is in Otto's Latin prose
greek: Codex a Baane, notario Aretae archiepiscopi Caesariensis, anno Christi 914 exaratus est. [Otto's Latin, read from the OCR text layer.] Title as OCR-printed by Otto: ᾿4ϑηναγόρου ἀϑηναίου φιλοσόφου χρισειανοῦ πρεσβεία περὶ χριστιανῶν (fol. 322b of the codex).
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena 1857), Prolegomena p. xiii, read from the OCR text layer of the scan archive.org/details/corpusapologeta03moragoog (Google scan; pdftotext output, OCR errors possible)
english: Latin/English for secondary source: my own reading of Otto's Latin (not a translation)
page: Otto Prolegomena p. xiii (scan PDF p. 266 of the _text.pdf; header read as 'xiii')
edition: Otto 1857 vol. VII (scan: Google/archive.org 'corpusapologeta03moragoog', dated 1969 in metadata)
what_it_says: Otto reports that Paris gr. 451, containing Athenagoras's Embassy and De resurrectione, was written by Baanes, notary of Arethas archbishop of Caesarea, in AD 914.
use: context / supports the claim that Arethas's circle preserved Athenagoras (the 914 date is Otto's, from the colophon/palaeography)
limits: Arethas is named as the notary's employer, not as author or owner of the codex; the 914 date is Otto's own dating. Otto dates Par. 1 to the 10th/early 11th c. and says the Athenagoras title is of a later hand than the original (recentioris aetatis, perhaps 11th c.).

ref: Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 4.3 (negative check: HE 1-9 and 4.23 region)
english: Aristides also, a believer earnestly devoted to our religion, left, like Quadratus, an apology for the faith, addressed to Adrian.
translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1, as named on the newadvent page)
page: page unknown (NPNF2 vol. 1, Eusebius HE book 4 chapter 3)
edition: NPNF2 vol. 1 (Schaff & Wace, Buffalo 1890) via newadvent
what_it_says: Eusebius names Quadratus and Aristides as second-century apologists but the Athenagoras name does not appear in HE books 1-9 (checked by full-text search of newadvent pages 250101-250109).
use: negative result: supports 'Eusebius is silent about Athenagoras'
limits: Book 10 page did not load (not checked). Eusebius's Chronicle and other works not checked. Silence is an argument from absence only.

ref: Jerome, De viris illustribus 23 (Justin Martyr) with the Athenagoras addressee problem
english: Justin, a philosopher, and wearing the garb of philosopher, a citizen of Neapolis ... He addressed another book also to the successors of this Antoninus, Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.
translator: Ernest Cushing Richardson (NPNF2 vol. 3, as named on newadvent)
what_it_says: Jerome attributes to Justin a work addressed to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, the addressees of Athenagoras's Embassy.
use: objection-background: the Embassy's addressees appear in a Jerome entry under Justin, a possible source of misattribution (secondary-source reading)
limits: Jerome's wording is ambiguous; the Wikisource DCB entry (secondary) says Jerome may mean Athenagoras, and argues he means Justin's Lesser Apology. Not decided here.

ref: Jerome, De viris illustribus (full chapter list 1-135, negative check)
english: (negative result) No chapter headed Athenagoras among Jerome's 135 entries; the name occurs only as 'Athenian' (Aristides), 'Athens' (Quadratus, Dionysius) and 'Athenodorus'.
what_it_says: Jerome's De viris illustribus as printed on newadvent does not name Athenagoras; I found no Latin text to confirm the English list.
limits: Latin Wikisource page fetched returned no Athenagoras, but its text layer was not checked for chapter 23 or 24 Latin.
memory_only: Jerome's entries on Athenagoras are not in my memory; do not cite from memory

ref: Philip of Side, Fragment 2 (Cod. Barocc. 142), ed. Dodwell 1689 p. 488; GCS 54 (Hansen 1971) p. 160
greek_edition: Greek not read; Dodwell 1689 and Hansen GCS 54 cited by the tertullian.org page
english: Athenagoras was the first to lead the school in Alexandria; he flourished in the times of Hadrian and Antoninus, to whom also he addressed his Embassy-speech on behalf of the Christians—a man who lived as a Christian in the very philosophers' cloak, and who was at the head of the Academic school.
translator: Andrew Eastbourne (credit line on tertullian.org, Philip of Side Fragments page)
what_it_says: Philip claims Athenagoras preceded Pantaenus as head of the Alexandrian catechetical school.
use: objection (historical claim); the claim is judged probably incorrect and contradicted by Eusebius (Wikipedia; ANL intro, both secondary)
limits: Philip's notice is 5th c. and was extracted by an unknown writer; the page points to Pouderon 1997 ch. 1 for discussion. Only the English read; no Greek or Dodwell text read. Suidas not found in searches.

ref: Introductory notice to Athenagoras (Ante-Nicene Christian Library), on Methodius via Epiphanius Haer. 64 and Photius Bibl. 234
english: One of these occurs in the work of Methodius, On the Resurrection of the Body, as preserved by Epiphanius (Hær. lxiv.), and Photius (Biblioth. ccxxxiv.). The other notice of him is found in the writings of Philip of Side, in Pamphylia, who flourished in the early part of the fifth century.
translator: not identified in the text read (Ante-Nicene Christian Library, vol. 2, public domain)
edition: Ante-Nicene Christian Library, Clark, Edinburgh (1867 era; date not confirmed on page)
what_it_says: The only two early references to Athenagoras are a Methodius passage (preserved by Epiphanius and Photius) and Philip of Side.
use: reception: Methodius (d. 312) is the earliest witness (secondary claim; also Wikipedia: 'several accredited quotations from his Apology in a fragment of Methodius of Olympus')
limits: I did not read Photius cod. 234 or Epiphanius Haer. 64 directly. The ANL note also calls the Philip statement 'a more interesting and perhaps well-founded' point, but the headship claim 'probably incorrect'.

ref: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 234 (Methodius, On the Resurrection): not read
greek_edition: Bekker 1824 (archive.org bibliothecaexrec00photuoft): OCR unusable for Greek; Freese 1920 (archive.org libraryofphotius00phot): codex 234 not in the text layer I have
what_it_says: Negative/unverified: I could not read Photius cod. 234 and cannot confirm that it names Athenagoras. The claim that cod. 234 preserves Methodius on the Resurrection comes from the ANL introduction (secondary).
limits: The Freese copy stops before codex 234 in my OCR; Bekker OCR too poor. Migne PG 103 not checked.

greek_edition: Greek not recovered (Otto OCR unreadable here)
english: God begot before all creatures a Beginning, [who was] a certain rational power [proceeding] from Himself, who is called by the Holy Spirit, now the Glory of the Lord, now the Son, again Wisdom ...
what_it_says: Justin says God begot before creatures a rational power from Himself, called Logos, Son, Wisdom, and says the Word was begotten by an act of will.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Logos eternal in God, begotten before creation; parallels Leg. 10 'πρῶτον γέννημα' and the 'in idea and operation' pattern)
limits: Justin's ANF chapter names the Word as 'Beginning', 'Son', 'Wisdom', 'Glory of the Lord', 'Angel' and 'Lord and Logos'; the power is 'begotten ... by an act of will'. Pre-Nicene subordinationist wording in places; not Nicene in later terms.

english: Chapter 128. The Word is sent not as an inanimate power, but as a person begotten of the Father's substance
what_it_says: The power sent from the Father is said to be numerically distinct and begotten, not merely a light-like emanation.
use: answer to objection (against the 'mere emanation' view, as in Sabellian reading); supports Son as person
limits: The argument is Justin's own; the Sabellian/Arian charge is not directly quoted here. The 'person' wording is the ANF heading, not the Greek text.

english: But both Him, and the Son (who came forth from Him and taught us these things, and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him), and the prophetic Spirit, we worship and adore, knowing them in reason and truth.
what_it_says: Christians worship the Father, the Son who came forth from Him, the good angels, and the prophetic Spirit.
use: supports Trinitarian order of worship (Father, Son, Spirit); parallels Leg. 10/12 'Father, Son, Spirit' list
limits: The Son is grouped with 'the host of the other good angels'; the text does not say the Spirit is a person.

english: That we reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third, we will prove.
what_it_says: Justin's stated order is God, the Son in second place, the prophetic Spirit in third.
use: supports 'rank' (taxis) distinction in Leg. 12 'their distinction in rank'
limits: 'second place' and 'third' are in the ANF English; the Greek word for place (τάξις?) not read.

greek: ὑπόστασις; διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως (Greek words as printed in the ANF English, not full Greek text)
greek_edition: Greek words as printed by the ANF editor, not read from Greek edition
english: God was in the beginning; but the beginning, we have been taught, is the power of the Logos ... by His simple will the Logos springs forth; and the Logos, not coming forth in vain, becomes the first-begotten work of the Father ... He came into being by participation, not by abscission
what_it_says: The Logos comes forth by the Father's will and becomes the first-begotten work, without abscission.
use: supports prolation/generation pattern close to Leg. 10 ('πρῶτον γέννημα', 'not as having been made')
limits: Tatian's 'first-begotten work' is a creature-like wording (Arian-prone); not a Nicene formula.

english: God, then, having His own Word internal within His own bowels, begot Him, emitting Him along with His own wisdom before all things.
what_it_says: The Word is internal in God, then begotten and emitted with Wisdom.
use: supports endiathetos/prophorikos pattern as in Leg. 10 'Logos in Himself' and 'came forth'
limits: Pre-Nicene 'emission' language; the internal/uttered distinction is the Stoic background.

english: In like manner also the three days which were before the luminaries, are types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom.
what_it_says: Theophilus uses a triad of God, Word and Wisdom, applied to the three days before the luminaries.
use: supports 'Triad' word in pre-Nicene writers (the brief's 'Trinity' term may be the translator's, not Theophilus's)
limits: The term 'Trinity' is the translator's rendering; Greek not read, so the Greek word is unverified. Word and Wisdom are not 'persons' in Nicene sense.

english: For before anything came into being He had Him as a counsellor, being His own mind and thought. But when God wished to make all that He determined on, He begot this Word, uttered, the first-born of all creation, not Himself being emptied of the Word [Reason].
what_it_says: The Word is God's own mind before creation and was uttered at creation, as first-born of creation.
use: supports 'in idea' (endiathetos) and 'energy' (prophorikos) pattern; parallel to Leg. 10 'ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ' and 'πρῶτον γέννημα'
limits: Stoic-style emission model; Theophilus says 'first-born of all creation' (creature-like wording).

english: 4.20.3: I have also largely demonstrated, that the Word, namely the Son, was always with the Father; and that Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation.
what_it_says: The Son is always with the Father; Wisdom, which Irenaeus calls the Spirit, was present with Him before creation.
use: supports eternal co-presence of Son and Spirit (identifies Spirit with Wisdom, a Logos/Wisdom reading)
limits: Irenaeus identifies Spirit with Wisdom, not with the Father's effluence; the Greek original is lost and only Latin/English survive.

english: The Catholic Doctrine of the Trinity and Unity ... this one only God has also a Son, His Word, who proceeded from Himself, by whom all things were made.
what_it_says: Tertullian states the 'economy' view: one God with Son and Word who proceeded from the Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading of 'the Son proceeded' (parallel to Leg. 10 'came forth')
limits: Tertullian's 'proceeded' and 'economy' are not the Nicene 'consubstantial' formula; Praxeas is the Monarchian opponent (a Sabellian-type reading).

greek: προβολή (Greek word as printed in the ANF English)
greek_edition: Greek word as printed by the ANF page, not read from Greek
english: If any man from this shall think that I am introducing some προβολή — that is to say, some prolation of one thing out of another, as Valentinus does ... Truth must not therefore refrain from the use of such a term ... Was the Word of God put forth or not?
what_it_says: Tertullian defends the term prolation for the Son's emission from the Father, against Valentinian separation.
use: answer to objection (the Valentinian/Arian 'separation' charge: the Word is put forth but not separated)
limits: Tertullian's answer uses the Valentinian term; the Latin text not read. The same worry about separability attaches to Athenagoras's 'comes forth' (Leg. 10).
